title: The Spirit prays (Romans 8:26–27)
hook: we don't know how to pray, and the Spirit asks for us with groanings

segments.voice: Yesterday, wretched: the good I would, and the evil I would not. Your line was who shall deliver me.

A hospital waiting room at three in the morning. A woman sits with her coat still on; her husband is in surgery. She wants to pray and has no idea what to say. Heal him? Give me strength? Let it be quick? Nothing she knows by heart seems to fit. All she has is a long breath out. Paul wrote about a moment like that, and he didn't call it a failure.
screen: `A WAITING ROOM, 3 A.M.` → `NO WORDS COME.` → `ONLY A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: After chapter seven's cry, who shall deliver me, chapter eight opens with no condemnation, and then it's full of the Spirit. All creation groans, Paul says, like a woman in labor, waiting. We groan too. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity. For we know not what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings." Three things. First, Paul includes himself: we know not what to pray for. The apostle whose name is on so many New Testament letters admits he doesn't always know how to pray. Second, the Spirit helps our infirmity, our weakness. The Greek verb pictures someone taking hold of the other end of a heavy load. The one who prays isn't carrying it alone. Third, unspeakable groanings. Too deep for words. The Spirit's own prayer sounds less like a speech and more like a sigh. The next verse adds that God, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit means, because the Spirit asks according to God's will. So, on Paul's reading, the wordless sigh in the waiting room is not a failed prayer. It's a prayer the Spirit carries. The Catechism quotes this passage when it calls the Holy Spirit the interior master of Christian prayer.
screen: `CREATION GROANS, AND SO DO WE.` · `WE KNOW NOT WHAT TO PRAY FOR.` · `THE SPIRIT TAKES THE OTHER END.` · `UNSPEAKABLE GROANINGS.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT PRAYS FOR US.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whatever is heaviest right now, something you don't know how to pray about, and don't look for words. Breathe in slowly, then let out a long sigh, out loud if you can, and let it carry the whole thing; do it again. If you pray, rest in Paul's picture of the Spirit asking, in that breath, what you can't; if not, notice how much a sigh can hold.
Groanings. What the Spirit prays in us when we don't know how, too deep for words, carrying the other end of the load. Today's word.
Your line: the spirit prays for us. A sigh can be a whole prayer. Day five hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics often begin prayer by asking the Holy Spirit's help, and the Church teaches that the Spirit is the interior teacher of prayer; some pray in silence, without words, before the Blessed Sacrament.

fork.setup: you're in a waiting room in the middle of the night. you want to pray and no words come. what do you do?
options: give up; it doesn't count without words.
let a sigh be the prayer.
look up the right prayer first.
fork.reveal: not graded. but Paul says the Spirit asks for us with unspeakable groanings, and God knows what the Spirit means.

original.note: Greek: with groanings that cannot be spoken, sighs too deep for words.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer is finding the right words.
what it means: when we don't know what to pray, the Spirit prays in us with sighs deeper than words, and God understands.
what a scholar hears: synantilambanetai, helpeth, pictures taking hold together on the other end of a load. the groaning echoes the groaning of creation and of believers just before.

chat.meaning: In Romans 8, the Spirit helps our weakness and asks for us with unspeakable groanings; a wordless sigh is a prayer the Spirit carries.
